S054-01.notes: The appositive 'avoiding dramatic language and acknowledging the arguments on every side' defines a restrained, balanced tone, so 'measured' fits, and the 'Though...bold' contrast also works with it. A 'exhaustive' describes thoroughness, not tone, and nothing in the text supports it. B 'belated' is about timing, not tone. D 'partisan' contradicts 'acknowledging the arguments on every side'.

S054-02.notes: Both groups got the same inactive pill and were randomly assigned. The only difference was the warning, so expectation explains the gap. B fails because the pill is inactive and was the same for both groups. C overreaches with 'should never', which is a policy claim. D fails because random assignment rules out differences that existed before the study.

S054-03.notes: 4% of 200,000 = 8,000 and 6% of 300,000 = 18,000. That is 2.25 times as many, so the number more than doubled, while the share rose from 4 to 6 percent, which is an increase of one half. D is the only choice that gives both parts of the claim. A gives only the share. B gives only the workforce growth. C gives only the 2023 count, with no baseline to show doubling.

S054-04.notes: The last sentence states the thesis: guilds had mixed effects that depended on how each one was governed. A is the old view that the text revises. C picks out only one example and overstates it with 'chiefly responsible'. D twists a detail: the text says standards let distant buyers trust unfamiliar goods, not that buyers distrusted outside goods as a main point.

flags.note: The item tests who vs. whom. College Board generally keeps who/whom off its Standard English Conventions blueprint because 'who' as an object is widely accepted, so this is borderline off-blueprint. The key is still correct under formal convention: 'the library hired [whom]'.

S054-05.notes: Inserted: 'The archivist whom the library hired last spring has already digitized...' The relative pronoun is the object of 'hired', so 'whom' is correct. B 'who' is the subject form, which is informal here. C 'whose ... hired' leaves 'whose' with no noun to modify and does not work. D 'which' is used for things, not a person.

S054-06.notes: This is an inverted past counterfactual: 'Had the engineers examined' = 'If the engineers had examined', which pairs with 'would have noticed'. A 'Had the engineers examine' is ungrammatical after the auxiliary 'had'. B 'Had ... have examined' doubles the auxiliary. D 'examines' is a finite present-tense verb that does not agree with the plural subject and cannot follow 'had'.

S054-07.notes: The surprising finding is that colonies unable to read the dance did about as well in some seasons. B sets that against what the dance is for ('Though the dance shows where food is'). A gives background with no finding. C is the expected result, so it is not surprising. D describes the method only, with no result.

S054-08.notes: Text 2 offers another explanation: red signals chemical defenses to egg-laying insects. The ecologists would therefore say red may serve a different function, and nothing indicates they reject Text 1 outright. B is too absolute, since Text 2 never addresses sunlight protection. C wrongly ties the regional pattern to sunscreen when Text 2 explains it by insects. D: Text 2 says nothing about yellow-leaved trees or nutrient recovery.
